title: What is Data Science?
q: What is data science?
a: A definition, a mechanism, and a consequence. 'Data science turns data into decisions by combining statistics, computation and domain knowledge; the deliverable is a claim with evidence and quantified uncertainty; it differs from BI because it answers whether a difference is real, not just what happened.'

title: What is Data Science?
q: Difference between a data analyst and a data scientist?
a: Analyst: describes and diagnoses using existing tools (SQL, BI, Excel), owns reporting and experimentation monitoring. Scientist: additionally builds predictive/statistical models and often owns the question design. Mention that the boundary moves by company - senior candidates always say that.

title: What is Data Science?
q: How would you start a project where the stakeholder says 'make sense of our data'?
a: Refuse the vague brief politely: ask which decision is blocked. Then propose 2-3 candidate questions, pick one with the stakeholder, define success metric, baseline and shape of the deliverable before touching data.

title: Data Analyst vs Data Scientist vs ML Engineer vs AI Engineer
q: Why do you want to be a data scientist?
a: Use evidence not adjectives: name a project, the decision it informed, and the skill you are currently deepening. Avoid 'I love data'.

title: Data Analyst vs Data Scientist vs ML Engineer vs AI Engineer
q: Difference between data scientist and ML engineer?
a: Scientist owns the question, validation and communication (offline, experimental). ML engineer owns training/serving pipelines, reliability and latency (on call). Overlap exists; the on-call question settles it.

title: Data Analyst vs Data Scientist vs ML Engineer vs AI Engineer
q: What does an AI engineer do that an ML engineer does not?
a: AI engineers build products around foundation models: retrieval, prompting, tool use, evaluation harnesses, cost/latency control and safety. They often do not train models at all, and their core discipline is evaluation.

title: The Data Science Workflow
q: Walk me through how you approach a new data science project.
a: Structure the answer on artefacts: problem statement with decision owner and baseline -> data dictionary and quality report -> analysis-ready table -> baseline model -> candidate models with cross-validation -> business validation -> deployment and monitoring. Mention one project where evaluation sent you back to framing.

title: The Data Science Workflow
q: How do you define success before modelling?
a: Three layers: business KPI, statistical criterion (minimum detectable effect), model metric chosen by error cost. Name the error cost asymmetry explicitly - it justifies precision/recall trade-offs.

title: The Data Science Workflow
q: What is data leakage and where does it usually enter?
a: Information available at training time that will not be available at prediction time. Common entries: target-derived features, fitting scalers on the full dataset, temporal splits done randomly, and join columns that encode the outcome. Day 166 and Day 195 give the defences.

title: Setting Up Your Python Environment
q: What is a virtual environment and why does it matter?
a: An isolated interpreter + package set. It matters for reproducibility and dependency isolation: each project pins its own versions, so upgrading one project cannot break another, and CI can rebuild the same state.

title: Setting Up Your Python Environment
q: requirements.txt vs environment.yml?
a: requirements.txt is a pip pin list (usually `pip freeze`) - exact versions, Python-only. environment.yml is conda's export and can include the interpreter version, channels and non-Python libraries (e.g. CUDA-linked builds). Use conda for the base, pip inside for pure-Python packages, and commit both.

title: Setting Up Your Python Environment
q: How do you make a data project reproducible for a colleague?
a: Pin the interpreter and packages, seed randomness, snapshot the data (or document the exact query/extraction date), document the run order in a README, and keep notebooks restart-and-run-all clean.

title: Jupyter, Colab, Packages and Reproducibility
q: When would you use a notebook and when a script?
a: Notebook for exploration, visual iteration and communication; script/module for anything reused, tested, scheduled or deployed. The litmus test: if it must run the same way twice, it does not belong only in a notebook.

title: Jupyter, Colab, Packages and Reproducibility
q: What is the execution-order problem in notebooks and how do you mitigate it?
a: Kernel state persists across edits, so displayed outputs may not be reproducible from the saved file. Mitigations: restart-and-run-all before sharing, modularise logic into imports, and convert scheduled work into scripts with parameterised runs.

title: Jupyter, Colab, Packages and Reproducibility
q: How do you keep secrets out of notebooks?
a: Never hardcode; load from environment variables or a .env file that is gitignored; clear outputs before committing; rotate any key that was ever committed because history retains it.

title: Variables, Data Types and Operators
q: What happens when you write a = b for a list?
a: Both names reference the same object; no copy is made. Mutating through either name is visible through both. Copying requires b = a.copy() (shallow) or copy.deepcopy(a) (nested).

title: Variables, Data Types and Operators
q: Difference between `is` and `==`?
a: `is` compares identity (same object in memory - same id), `==` compares value equality via __eq__. Use `is` for None/singletons, `==` for values. Note CPython caches small ints and interns some strings, so `is` can appear to work for values - a trap not a rule.

title: Variables, Data Types and Operators
a: Floats are binary64; 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum carries representation error. Practical rule: use tolerances (isclose) or Decimal for money; never exact equality on computed floats.

title: Variables, Data Types and Operators
q: Explain mutable default arguments.
a: Defaults are evaluated once at function definition, so a mutable default is shared across calls and accumulates state. Use None as the sentinel and construct the container inside the body.

title: Strings in Depth
q: Why are Python strings immutable, and what practical consequence does that have?
a: Immutability allows safe sharing, hashing (dict keys) and thread safety. Practically, every 'modifying' method returns a new string, so loops that concatenate are quadratic - use join() instead.

title: Strings in Depth
q: How do you clean a numeric column that arrives as messy text?
a: Normalise unicode and whitespace, strip currency/unit text, remove thousands separators, then cast inside try/except with an explicit fallback. Validate the result (range, negatives) and log rows that failed.

title: Strings in Depth
q: What is the difference between split() and partition()?
a: split() returns a list (all parts, or n splits); partition() returns a 3-tuple (before, separator, after) and always yields three elements - useful for parsing a single delimiter safely.

title: Lists and Tuples
q: Difference between a list and a tuple?
a: List: mutable, dynamic array, used for homogeneous sequences you will modify. Tuple: immutable, hashable, used for fixed records (coordinates, DB rows) and as dict keys. Tuples are slightly smaller and faster.

title: Lists and Tuples
q: Why does `print(my_list.sort())` print None?
a: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None by convention (mutating methods return None to signal they changed state). Use sorted(list) if you need the result.

title: Lists and Tuples
q: What is the time complexity of appending to a list and of inserting at position 0?
a: Append is amortised O(1) thanks to over-allocation; insert at 0 is O(n) because every element shifts. For queue-like behaviour use collections.deque (O(1) at both ends).

title: Lists and Tuples
q: A colleague says 'I copied the DataFrame and the original changed anyway'. How do you explain it?
a: Copy semantics: plain assignment aliases, shallow copies share nested objects, and pandas has its own copy-on-write rules. In pandas 2.x you also get SettingWithCopyWarning for chained assignment. The general principle from lists and tuples generalises: know whether you hold a reference or a copy.

title: Sets and Dictionaries
q: When would you use a set instead of a list?
a: When uniqueness or fast membership matters: deduplication, 'which ids are new', set algebra between two sources. Lists when order or duplicates are meaningful.

title: Sets and Dictionaries
q: How do Python dictionaries achieve O(1) lookup?
a: They are hash tables: hash(key) maps to a bucket index, collisions are resolved by probing, and equality is checked on match. Keys must be hashable (immutable) so the hash never changes while the key lives in the table.

title: Sets and Dictionaries
q: Explain `d.get('k', [])` vs `d.setdefault('k', [])`.
a: get returns the default without inserting. setdefault inserts the default if the key is missing and returns the (possibly pre-existing) value - useful for grouping, though defaultdict and Counter are cleaner.

title: Sets and Dictionaries
q: How would you merge two dictionaries where the second should override the first, without mutating either?
a: {**a, **b} or a | b (3.9+). For nested configs you need a recursive merge; note that deep_merge is not in the stdlib, so write and test it explicitly.

title: Indexing and Slicing Mastery
q: What does `data[1:5]` return and why?
a: Four elements from index 1 up to but not including index 5. Python slices are start-inclusive, stop-exclusive, which makes length arithmetic clean: stop - start.

title: Indexing and Slicing Mastery
q: How do you reverse a sequence?
a: seq[::-1] creates a reversed copy. For large data prefer reversed(seq) or iterating backwards to avoid copying.

title: Indexing and Slicing Mastery
q: Why does modifying a NumPy slice change the original array but not for a Python list?
a: Lists are arrays of pointers, so slicing copies the pointer array (new list, shared objects). NumPy basic slicing returns a view over the same buffer with different strides; no data is copied. Fancy indexing does copy.

title: Indexing and Slicing Mastery
q: How would you take every third element starting from the second?
a: seq[1::3]: start at index 1, no stop, step 3.

title: Conditions and Branching Logic
q: Why does branch order matter in if/elif chains?
a: Because evaluation stops at the first True branch, so order encodes priority. Specific conditions must come before general ones or they become unreachable.

title: Conditions and Branching Logic
q: What is short-circuit evaluation and why is it useful?
a: and stops at the first falsy operand, or at the first truthy one. It lets you guard risky checks: `if df is not None and len(df) > 0`. It also makes `a or default` a safe fallback idiom.

title: Conditions and Branching Logic
q: How do you apply 1e6 rows of business rules efficiently?
a: Vectorise with np.select or pandas where/mask; both take the first matching condition per row so order is part of the policy. Python-level if/elif per row is 20-40x slower and belongs only in tests or small samples.

title: Conditions and Branching Logic
q: Difference between `==` and `is` for None?
a: `is` compares identity and is the correct test for None; `==` calls __eq__, which can be overridden, and NaN comparisons with == are always False.

title: Loops and Iteration Tools
q: When would you use a while loop instead of a for loop?
a: When the number of iterations is unknown: convergence, retry with backoff, draining a queue, reading a stream. Always add an upper bound so a logic error cannot hang the process.

title: Loops and Iteration Tools
q: What does the else clause on a for loop do?
a: It runs only if the loop completed without break - the idiom for 'not found' branches in search algorithms.

title: Loops and Iteration Tools
q: How do you speed up a nested loop in a data pipeline?
a: First remove the quadratic behaviour: build a dict/set for O(1) lookups, or join in SQL/pandas. Then vectorise with NumPy/pandas if the operation is elementwise. Measure both versions to prove the gain.

title: Loops and Iteration Tools
q: Why is iterating pandas rows considered bad practice?
a: iterrows boxes each value into Python objects and rebuilds a Series per row, losing dtype efficiency; it is 100-1000x slower than vectorised ops. Use itertuples or, better, a vectorised/grouped formulation.

title: Functions, Arguments and Scope
q: What is the difference between arguments and parameters?
a: Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the actual values supplied at call time. Positional arguments map by order, keyword arguments by name, and defaults fill the gaps.

title: Functions, Arguments and Scope
q: Why is `def f(items=[]):` dangerous?
a: Defaults are evaluated once at definition and stored on the function object, so the same list is reused and accumulates across calls. Default to None and construct inside.

title: Functions, Arguments and Scope
q: Explain LEGB scope.
a: Name resolution order: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. Assignments inside a function create locals, which is why reading an outer variable then assigning to it raises UnboundLocalError unless declared global/nonlocal.

title: Functions, Arguments and Scope
q: What makes a function 'pure' and why does it matter for data pipelines?
a: Purity = same inputs produce the same output with no side effects. Pure functions are trivially testable, safe to parallelise, cacheable and reproducible - all requirements for reliable ML pipelines.

title: Lambda, map, filter, Modules and Packages
q: When should you use a lambda versus a def?
a: Lambda for a short, single-use expression where the function is obvious in place (sort keys, small callbacks). def when it needs a name, a docstring, multiple statements, testing or a meaningful traceback.

title: Lambda, map, filter, Modules and Packages
q: Difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?
a: Comprehensions build the whole list in memory (O(n)); generator expressions yield lazily (O(1) extra memory). Generators can only be consumed once, which is the trade-off.

title: Lambda, map, filter, Modules and Packages
q: What does `if __name__ == '__main__':` do?
a: It separates library behaviour from script behaviour: the block runs only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported. It keeps imports side-effect free, which tests and pipelines depend on.

title: Lambda, map, filter, Modules and Packages
q: How would you organise reusable data code across ten notebooks?
a: A package (src/) with pure transform functions, an io module for loading, and configuration; notebooks import it. Version it in Git, test it in CI, and expose a CLI entry point for scheduled runs (Days 31-32, 265).

title: Exceptions, Debugging, Files, JSON and pathlib + Foundation Project
q: How do you handle malformed rows in a large file?
a: Fail softly per row: parse inside try/except, push failures into a quarantine list with a reason, continue processing, then report the failure count. Fail loudly at the file/schema level so corruption is never hidden.

title: Exceptions, Debugging, Files, JSON and pathlib + Foundation Project
q: Why is `with open(...)` important?
a: It guarantees the file is closed even if an exception occurs, flushes buffered writes, and releases the handle. Manual close() is skipped on error paths.

title: Exceptions, Debugging, Files, JSON and pathlib + Foundation Project
q: What does pathlib give you over os.path?
a: Path objects with operators (/), rich attributes (suffix, stem, parent), cross-platform behaviour, and methods like mkdir(exist_ok=True) and read_text(encoding=...) - fewer string bugs and clearer code.

title: Exceptions, Debugging, Files, JSON and pathlib + Foundation Project
q: How do you make a script safe to run twice?
a: Idempotency: overwrite (never blindly append) outputs, create directories with exist_ok=True, avoid duplicating rows, and assert output counts match expectations.
